work.title: Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone
work.creator: J. K. Rowling

summary: The reader is built to feel the wonder of a hidden world, to belong at Hogwarts with Harry's friends, and to chase a mystery with a twist.

need-to-breathe.why: The Devil's Snare and Quirrell's hands at Harry's throat give a brief catch of breath.

hungry.why: The Hogwarts feasts, treacle tart, roast potatoes, and the sweets trolley, are described to make the reader hungry, a famous effect.

full.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

thirsty.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

gassy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-poop.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

need-to-pee.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

sleepy.why: The book does not aim to lull.

nauseous.why: Nothing is built to sicken the reader.

urge-to-sneeze.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

urge-to-cough.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

dizzy.why: Harry's bucking broom and the dive for the Snitch are built to give a flicker of vertigo.

fatigued.why: The reader is not made to feel exertion.

pain.why: Harry's searing scar and Quirrell's blistering hands are built for a wince.

disgusted.why: Troll bogies on the wand, the troll's stink, and Voldemort's face on the back of a head are built for a child's delighted disgust.

itchy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

tickled.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

over-stimulated.why: Nothing is built to overwhelm the senses.

too-hot-too-cold.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel heat or cold.

afraid.why: Fluffy, the troll, the hooded figure in the forest, and Voldemort's face are built to frighten a young reader.

anxious.why: The reader is built to worry about Snape, the Stone, and the house points through the second half.

panic.why: The troll in the bathroom and the Devil's Snare give a brief rush of panic.

sensory-pleasures.why: Feasts, Chocolate Frogs, and the feel of flying are built to give the reader vicarious pleasure.

aesthetic-pleasures.why: The Great Hall's ceiling and Diagon Alley are built as pleasures of imagined beauty.

piquancy.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

fun-excitement.why: Quidditch, flying lessons, wizard chess, and the trapdoor obstacles are built as pure fun, the book's main offer.

orgasm.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

love-romantic.why: Nothing is built to make the reader feel romantic love.

love-family.why: The Mirror of Erised and Mrs Weasley's sweater are built to touch the reader's own family feeling.

grief.why: Harry before the Mirror is built to make the reader feel the loss of parents never known.

missing-someone.why: The Mirror scene is built to make the reader share Harry's longing.

aroused-sexually.why: Nothing is built to arouse the reader.

liking-as-a-friend.why: The reader is built to love Ron, Hermione, and Hagrid as friends, the series' core appeal.

empathy.why: The reader is placed with the boy under the stairs and feels every slight and every wonder with him.

compassion.why: Harry's cupboard, Neville's bullying, and Hagrid's tears over Norbert are built to produce pity.

grateful.why: Nothing is built to make the reader grateful.

pleasure-from-helping.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

trustful-distrustful.why: The reader is led to distrust Snape and trust Quirrell, and the twist punishes it.

depressed.why: Nothing is built to lower the reader's mood.

angry.why: The Dursleys' cruelty and Snape's unfairness are built to anger the reader.

envious.why: Nothing is built to produce envy.

jealous-romantic-sexual.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

jealous-friendship.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

hatred.why: Malfoy, the Dursleys, and apparently Snape are built to be disliked, and Voldemort to be hated.

contempt.why: Dudley's tantrums, Vernon's bluster, and Malfoy's sneers are built for the reader's scorn.

resentment.why: Snape docking points and the Dursleys' injustice are built to make the reader feel unfairness.

proud.why: Gryffindor's Cup gives the reader a borrowed glow of pride.

amused.why: Dudley's pig tail, Fred and George, Peeves, and Hagrid's comic lines are built for laughter.

sense-of-belonging.why: The book is built to make the reader feel sorted into a house and at home at Hogwarts, its signature effect.

lonely.why: Harry's years at the Dursleys are built to make the reader feel his isolation before Hogwarts cures it.

judgy-moral-sense.why: The reader judges the Dursleys, Malfoy, and Snape, and is asked to admire Neville's stand.

admiration.why: Dumbledore, Hagrid, and Hermione's brains are built to be admired.

embarrassed.why: Harry's blushing fame and Neville's mishaps give secondhand embarrassment.

shame.why: Nothing is built to shame the reader.

guilt.why: Nothing is built to make the reader guilty.

sad.why: The Mirror and the return to the Dursleys give a sadness the book keeps light.

happy.why: Hogwarts life is built to make the reader happy, which is why readers return to it.

joyful-euphoric.why: The Snitch nearly swallowed and the House Cup reversal are built as bursts of joy.

effort.why: The book is built to be effortless.

focused-in-flow.why: The book is built as a page-turner that holds a child reader rapt.

distracted.why: The Snape red herring is built to distract the reader from Quirrell.

impatient.why: The reader waits with Harry for the letter and for Snape to be caught.

curious.why: Who is Nicolas Flamel, what is in vault 713, what does Fluffy guard: the book is built on the reader's questions.

surprised.why: Quirrell at the Mirror instead of Snape is built as the twist, and the House Cup reversal as a second.

awe.why: Diagon Alley, the castle across the lake, and the Great Hall are built to produce wonder, the book's first gift.

skeptical-doubtful.why: The reader is built to suspect Snape and to doubt Hagrid's faith in him.

feeling-of-knowing.why: The Flamel card is built so the reader, like Harry, feels the name is familiar before it is placed.

frustrated.why: The burned letters and the Dursleys' obstruction are built to frustrate the reader.

uncertain-certain.why: The reader is kept uncertain who the thief is until the Mirror chamber.

understanding.why: Dumbledore's explanation of the Mirror and Lily's love is built to make the plot click into place.

inspired.why: The idea of a hidden magical world is built to fire the reader's imagination.

satisfied.why: The Stone destroyed, the Cup won, and Harry's summer threat to Dudley close the book with full satisfaction.

foreboding.why: Harry's dreams of green light and the centaurs' warnings are built to make the reader expect worse.

nostalgia.why: The school year's rhythms are built to make older readers nostalgic for their own.

anticipation-suspense.why: The trapdoor obstacles and the Quidditch match are built as suspense a child can bear.

hope.why: The reader hopes for the letter, for Gryffindor, and for Harry's happiness.

schadenfreude.why: Dudley's pig tail, Malfoy's detention, and Snape's limp are built to be enjoyed.

elevation.why: Ron's sacrifice, Neville's courage, and Lily's love are built to lift the reader.

infatuation.why: Nothing is built to produce this.

rage.why: Vernon's bluster may provoke a flash of rage in the reader.
